name: Dana Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential; I’d like both the line you say publicly and your private view. What does a normal day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Dana, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company that makes water-quality dashboards. I have a bachelor’s degree and handle ordinary code faults well, while the hardest sensor rules go to our specialist. I start with an odd reading, compare the sensor record with lab results, and check the fix before it reaches a customer. I have never used AI tools; a clean graph can still hide a bad reading.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does this work sit with life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Priya, dispatches buses, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is high for the job, and we have roughly eight months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby. We built the reserve slowly, so I am careful about spending it on guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves us checking lab results against sensor graphs. A quick sorter is fine, but someone should sign the reading before a warning goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel secure about my pay and the mortgage. Eight months saved and local openings give us room for a normal setback, even if Priya’s dispatch shifts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking odd sensor readings with the lab sheet and ask the specialist to review unusual spikes. I’d leave our 450 monthly savings transfer in place while both incomes hold. In the first year I’d ask the team to keep a named reviewer on every public warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own work and pay. I still take bad water readings seriously, but I do not see this picture shrinking our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which sensor reading made you stop a notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sensor once showed a sudden clean reading while the lab sample was still poor. A clean graph can still hide a bad reading. I held the notice and found a calibration error before anyone relied on the graph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Priya the same household budget we use now. I would not treat the eight-month reserve as spare cash for a bigger car.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking lab results against sensor graphs.
I would keep a **named reviewer** on public warnings.
think: I expect my **pay and mortgage** to remain secure.
Our **eight-month reserve** and nearby jobs allow a normal setback.
do: **Keep** checking sensor spikes against lab sheets and specialist review.
**Transfer** 450 monthly into savings while both incomes hold.
**Require** a named reviewer before a public water warning goes out.
feel: **Calm** about household income, with care for correct warnings.
S0.quote: A clean graph can still hide a bad reading.
fieldNote: Her **manual cross-check** caught a calibration error before a public warning could rely on the misleading clean graph.
High pay, **eight months saved** and many local jobs support current financial security.

steps.text: Keep checking odd water-sensor graphs against lab sheets
Transfer 450 monthly into savings while both incomes hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could write code, check records and plan dispatch routes faster. I would ask management to show test results and staffing plans before setting new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our dashboard team could lose one developer, perhaps me. Priya’s route-planning work could also shrink, so our savings do not remove the household risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have our specialist run the approved AI checker over fifteen past calibration faults while I compare lab sheets. If it catches all fifteen, I’d learn to review its output during paid time. In the first year, if either employer announces cuts, I’d attend our local worker council meeting to press for notice and paid transition time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our own incomes, despite the reserve. I can learn a proven tool. If my tech company and my partner’s bus employer both cut jobs, our mortgage calculation changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the worker council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the calibration case that made a false clean reading to the meeting. A staffing target should not decide whether a warning is checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya about dispatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Priya to ask how dispatch errors are reviewed before her employer changes routes. We would compare written plans, not rumours at the bus stop.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, records and route planning.
I would demand **test results** and staffing plans before targets change.
think: I fear a **dashboard cut** could include me.
I worry Priya’s **dispatch planning** could shrink at the same time.
do: **Test** an approved checker against fifteen old calibration faults with the specialist.
**Learn** its review output during paid time only if all fifteen cases pass.
**Attend** the worker council if either employer announces cuts.
feel: **Anxious** about two possible income cuts despite eight months saved.
S1.quote: If my tech company and my partner’s bus employer both cut jobs, our mortgage calculation changes.
fieldNote: She will test **fifteen real faults** before using a new checker, with paid learning time.
Her **worker council** action requires announced cuts and addresses simultaneous household risk.

steps.text: Learn approved sensor-checker review during paid time if fifteen old cases pass
Attend worker council if either employer announces cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches water-dashboard code and dispatch planning in 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, but both our jobs involve thinking work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer role could end and Priya’s dispatch hours could fall. Eight months of savings is useful, but it will not buy two replacement wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask both employers for written staffing and severance terms now. I’d hold the planned larger-car deposit in savings and keep the current car safe. In the first year after 2028, if my role ends, I’d apply for actual local openings and eligible income help rather than assume another developer job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make a budget, but I expect a big loss of income and cannot see which employer would still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the larger car can wait while their school travel stays paid. I would not tell them the mortgage is lost before we know the facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the worker council have a role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the worker council to compare severance terms across both employers if cuts happen. I would not sign a settlement without seeing the written terms.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach dashboard code and dispatch planning before robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues **both desk jobs** face the earlier date.
think: I expect my **developer role** could end and Priya’s hours could fall.
Our **eight-month savings** cannot buy two replacement wages.
do: **Delay** the larger-car purchase and keep its deposit for bills.
**Request** written terms; ask worker council to compare severance if cuts happen.
**Apply** for actual local openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected income loss across both jobs.
S2.quote: Eight months of savings is useful, but it will not buy two replacement wages.
fieldNote: Both adults face **thinking-work change** in 2028; later robots offer little protection to their current roles.
She keeps the **car deposit**, seeks real jobs and makes public help conditional on eligibility.

steps.text: Delay buying a larger family car and hold its deposit for bills
Apply for actual local jobs if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028
Ask worker council to compare severance terms if cuts happen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to record how warnings and dispatch decisions are made. Thinking AI reaches our code and Priya’s planning in 2031; robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect a smaller dashboard team, but five years gives me room to learn lab quality rules while earning. I cannot assume lab review will remain a paid job after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one approved afternoon monthly with the lab lead learning how samples are checked. I’d use the free quality manual if the company refuses that time, and keep examples of errors I can now explain. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply for actual lab-support vacancies only if pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my job, though five years lets me try a real skill before making a move. I would keep most of our reserve for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove you learned lab quality?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lab lead to mark one explanation I got wrong. If I cannot explain the false clean reading, I should not claim I can review warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya and I would keep the children in their current school unless a real job offer pays for any move. We would not turn our savings into relocation money on an advert.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to document warnings and decisions.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier thinking-work change.
think: I expect a **smaller dashboard team** despite more warning.
I cannot assume **lab review** stays paid after full thinking AI.
do: **Learn** sample checks monthly if the company approves lab time.
**Study** the free quality manual if approved time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying lab-support openings if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about coding income, with time and savings to test another skill.
S3.quote: I cannot assume lab review will remain a paid job after full thinking AI.
fieldNote: Her **lab learning** requires approved time or a free manual, and error explanations supply evidence.
The **family move** depends on a real offer covering the mortgage and school change.

steps.text: Learn lab sample checks monthly with approval, or study free quality manual
Apply for actual lab-support jobs covering mortgage if coding ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to make warning rules easier to inspect. Thinking AI reaches dashboard code and dispatch planning in 2036; robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our wages to hold for the next few years, and our savings give us room to argue for a fair plan. AGI by 2036 should not postpone staffing talks today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking sensor readings against lab sheets and document one calibration rule each month. I’d continue saving 450 monthly while both wages hold. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d search real local openings and compare pay before moving the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about long-term work, though our mortgage feels secure for now. I want a written plan before anybody quietly reduces the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the worker council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the monthly rule notes to our worker council and ask how many experienced developers the firm expects to keep. I would not treat a software forecast as a staffing answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you revisit the car purchase?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya and I would keep the current car until an actual need and budget justify a replacement. We would not spend eight months of savings because a future date feels far away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code and Priya’s dispatch planning could shrink together. Written severance, paid time to learn lab rules and income help we qualify for would help. The reserve would buy us months to decide, not a second salary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns a clean-looking water graph when the lab sample says otherwise. A water warning that never goes out still affects the family drinking the water.

headlineQuote: A water warning that never goes out still affects the family drinking the water.
portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, high pay and eight months of expenses saved.
She has **never used AI** and checks water-sensor graphs against lab sheets before warnings reach customers.
Her partner’s **bus dispatch** faces thinking AI alongside her code, putting both wages at risk under fast AGI.
She seeks **written staffing terms**, approved lab learning and real openings while protecting mortgage cash.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut both her code pay and her partner’s dispatch hours.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning time and eligible income help would support the family.
